storyTitle: GitHub now open to everyone. Here is the pricing.
outcome: Acquired by Microsoft for $7.5B in 2018; 100M+ developers.
outcomeDetail: GitHub turned hosted Git into the default home for open source and grew past 100 million developer accounts. Microsoft paid $7.5 billion for it in 2018. The cheap virtual server it was compared to never became the developer network.
note: The confusion was understandable in 2008: GitHub was a paid Git host with a social layer. The social layer was the product, and it compounded.

author: khet
cardQuote: The copy is inferior to the original in my mind and I will never see the app as an equal.
quote: There are a couple reasons app developers should strive for originality. Copying Github's design only reminds me of how your app is second to Github. That Github was the one who thought of the beautiful interface and that by using your app I will be using a copy and not the original. The copy is inferior to the original in my mind and I will never see the app as an equal. This really dampens the excitement I have for it because it might never be able to compete with the experience Github provides. Another example is Open Office, everyone uses it and it does the job. But no one loves it, because its a copy. Its not the original and it will never be the same as using MS Office. Now compare that with Apple's iWork. Its not a copy; its an original. When I use it, I feel comfortable in knowing that Apple has worked to provide an experience that is second to none.
storyTitle: GitLab, open source github clone, reaches 3.0
outcome: IPO'd on Nasdaq in 2021; ~$15B market cap on debut.
outcomeDetail: GitLab kept the GitHub-like interface but won on self-hosting, CI, and an open-core model. It listed on Nasdaq in October 2021 and was valued at roughly $15 billion on its first day of trading.
note: The design-debt critique was fair. GitLab's ownership and deployment model mattered more than originality.

author: Alupis
cardQuote: Docker is built on-top of existing Linux technologies, mainly LXC, making it more-or-less disposable in the future (as someone else figures out how to abstract/manage LXC better)
quote: My gripes: * half git-syntax/half package manager-syntax is cumbersome to me. * Inability to compile Docker from source without using the Docker Project's provided "black box" binary Docker. * No formal explanation of how to create your own base image from scratch (ie. not using a Docker Project provided base image). * Defaults to storing images in the Docker "cloud" repo. (would have preferred a git-like setup where pushing my images to a repo of my choice was more "normal") * GO Lang is still pretty obscure for most developers, and an interesting choice given the language's youth and likely-hood to change rapidly as it matures. * Docker is built on-top of existing Linux technologies, mainly LXC, making it more-or-less disposable in the future (as someone else figures out how to abstract/manage LXC better) * Docker is mainly built by Dotcloud - a for-profit company. Dotcloud has been very generous in their effort... but, being for-profit, what is their take out of it? (It can't be "just for the goodness of Linux").
storyTitle: Docker 1.0
outcome: Containers became the default deployment unit; Docker's image format is ubiquitous.
outcomeDetail: Docker did not get abstracted away. Its image format, Dockerfile, and registry became the standard packaging layer for cloud software, and Kubernetes adopted the same container model. Docker Inc. had a rocky business history, but Docker the tool won.
note: The LXC point was technically right—Docker replaced LXC with libcontainer. The conclusion that this made Docker disposable was wrong.

author: anonjon
cardQuote: What exactly is the driving force behind the desire to do everything in Javascript? Is it just because we have a surplus of Javascript programmers? It doesn't seem to me that this task is particularly well suited to Javascript.
quote: What exactly is the driving force behind the desire to do everything in Javascript? Is it just because we have a surplus of Javascript programmers? It doesn't seem to me that this task is particularly well suited to Javascript. (I think) Something like Erlang would be more applicable. And to me it seems that learning a new programming language (even one using a relatively obscure syntax), is a much simpler task than designing an entire project (or piece of a project), around a language that doesn’t really fit the needs of a project. To that extent, I think that the idea of a ‘lingua franca’ language is an inherently broken metaphor. Programming languages are closer to human-computer interaction tools than they are natural languages. ‘Lingua franca’ implies that every language can communicate approximately the same thing (it is just a matter of who has influence). I think this is a mistake, as different languages allow you to think in hugely different ways about programming. Different languages have different intrinsic concepts. It may be that this argument boils down to ‘if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail,’ but even that is an oversimplification, as I don’t even use the same hammer for all types of nails (tack hammer, framing hammer, etc). I am not saying that node.js is necessarily a bad thing to have. It may turn out that Javascript is indeed particularly well suited to this type of application. Superficially, however, nothing convinces me that this is some sort of exciting home-run-win situation (or that it is any better than any other functional-style programming language). Could you explain the excitement and appeal to me?
storyTitle: Node.js is genuinely exciting
outcome: One of the most-used runtimes; npm became the largest package ecosystem.
outcomeDetail: Node.js made JavaScript a first-class server language and now underpins a huge share of web tooling. The npm registry it spawned grew to more than a million packages and tens of billions of monthly downloads.
note: The 'just a surplus of JavaScript programmers' theory missed the real advantage: one language across client and server, with an event loop built for I/O.

author: prodigal_erik
cardQuote: The obvious question is how much work it'll be to turn each NPM into a system package for production use.
quote: The obvious question is how much work it'll be to turn each NPM into a system package for production use. It took us months to straighten out a nest of servers which had assorted unique versions of code smuggled onto them with ad hoc single-language tools completely lacking RPM integration, and we're not about to go there again. The sample package.json doesn't show any way to list native (non-node) dependencies, which is not a good sign.
storyTitle: Node NPM rocks
outcome: Acquired by GitHub in 2020; 75B monthly downloads.
outcomeDetail: npm became the default package manager for Node.js and the largest software registry in the world. GitHub bought npm in 2020, when it was serving about 75 billion downloads a month.
note: The RPM-integration worry was real for ops teams. It did not stop npm from becoming the path of least resistance for JavaScript.

author: moe
cardQuote: It likes to be compared with MongoDB or TokyoTyrant but is clearly not playing in the same league. Moreover it glosses over this issue in quite a self-righteous fashion almost everywhere.
quote: Even without the persistence you can say something is a database. It's not a coincidence that the term "in memory database" exists for example. Then why is redis not advertised as an "in memory database"? It likes to be compared with MongoDB or TokyoTyrant but is clearly not playing in the same league. Moreover it glosses over this issue in quite a self-righteous fashion almost everywhere. One example of many would be this gem from the "TwitterAlikeExample": This means you can serve millions of users every day with just a single Linux box, and this one was monkey asses slow! That's just false advertising if your "millions of users" actually use the service. Just storing the plain account data for 1 million users would push the database into the 1GB realm. Go figure what happens when these users actually begin to leave a footprint. Btw everything is used to store data permantly, reliably or not for your specific needs/tastes, is a database. I'm not normally nitpicking about terminology. It just left a bad taste in my mouth in this particular case because the redis homepage doesn't bother to mention this critical difference to most similar offerings. The current blurb is highly deceptive.
storyTitle: MongoDB vs Redis, a different interpretation of what's wrong with Relational DBs
outcome: A standard in-memory data store; Redis Labs valued at $2B+ in 2021.
outcomeDetail: Redis became the default in-memory cache, queue, and session store for web infrastructure. Redis Labs, the company behind it, was valued at more than $2 billion in 2021 and reported 8,000+ paying customers.
note: The durability critique was legitimate. Redis's answer was to be excellent at the jobs where durability is not the point.

quote: MongoDB is a fun toy database right now, nothing more. Unless you have the resources to fix every problem that comes up, you should use a mature database like Postgres or MySQL (MySQL is not as terrible as some might think).
storyTitle: MongoDB and RocksDB at Parse

outcomeDetail: Elasticsearch became the default open-source search and logging engine, powering the ELK stack and countless observability products. Elastic took it public in 2018.

author: ry0ohki

storyTitle: Salesforce Buys Heroku (YC W08)  For $212 Million In Cash
outcome: Acquired by Salesforce for $212M; still operating 15 years later.
outcomeDetail: Salesforce bought Heroku in 2010 for $212 million. Heroku kept running as a PaaS and was still onboarding developers well past the five-year mark the comment set.
note: Heroku's growth did slow, and it became a cautionary tale about platform lock-in. But it outlived the five-year deadline by a decade.

author: mncolinlee

storyTitle: Ansible Simply Kicks Ass
outcome: Acquired by Red Hat for $126M in 2015; now part of IBM.
outcomeDetail: Ansible became one of the most widely used configuration-management tools and a core part of Red Hat's automation portfolio. Red Hat paid $126 million for it in 2015; IBM later acquired Red Hat.
note: Windows support was a real gap in 2013, and Ansible eventually added it. 'Dead on arrival' was a statement about one buyer's checklist, not the market.

author: peterwwillis
cardQuote: To be frank, any code monkey with a few weeks of free time to kill can create a tool that does exactly what this one does, and that's why there are dozens of them that all do the same thing, yet we always need a new one.... because they all stink at actually making things work better.
quote: tl;dr: Terraform is modular virtual infrastructure automation. [I would say it's an orchestration tool, but that usually implies datacenter-wide resources, and this just seems to apply to cloud service providers] "[..] Terraform combines resources from multiple services providers: we created a DigitalOcean Droplet and then used the IP address of that droplet to add a DNS record to DNSimple. This sort of infrastructure composition from code is new and extremely powerful." Well, "new" in the sense of "we created another thing to automate infrastructure deployment and configuration". I have worked with various amalgamated solutions that do this for the past 12 years. Of course they mention that in the software comparison section, but it doesn't take away from the fact that this isn't new by a long shot. "Terraform has a feature that is critical for safely iterating infrastructure: execution plans. Execution plans show you what changes Terraform plans on making to your infrastructure. [..] As a result, you know exactly what Terraform will do to your infrastructure to reach your desired state, and you can feel confident that Terraform won't surprise you in unexpected ways." So it's declarative, and it has a dry-run mode. The thing that really bugs me is the idea that you should be creating "code" to do rote tasks such as changing resources or deploying things. You know what the single most problematic thing about infrastructure changes is? Human error. It's a simple fact of user interface design that humans are less likely to fuck up a point-and-click interface than a command line program that you have to feed a hand-edited config to. And automated config generation can arguably be more error-prone. Automation/orchestration should not simply make things happen automatically. It should make things work more reliably, and require less expertise to do so. To be frank, any code monkey with a few weeks of free time to kill can create a tool that does exactly what this one does, and that's why there are dozens of them that all do the same thing, yet we always need a new one.... because they all stink at actually making things work better. This comic isn't just funny, it's a truism: https://xkcd.com/1319/
storyTitle: Terraform
outcome: HashiCorp IPO'd in 2021; IBM bought it for $6.4B in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Terraform became the de facto infrastructure-as-code tool across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. HashiCorp went public in 2021 and was acquired by IBM for $6.4 billion in 2025.
note: The 'another orchestration tool' critique was fair in a crowded field. Terraform's execution plan and multi-cloud provider model were the difference.

author: tyingq
cardQuote: I'm curious what protects Twilio from a race to the bottom in pricing from competitors. The barrier to entry here seems fairly low. There's Plivo, Nexmo, Tropo, Sinch, and probably others.
quote: I'm curious what protects Twilio from a race to the bottom in pricing from competitors. The barrier to entry here seems fairly low. There's Plivo, Nexmo, Tropo, Sinch, and probably others. Some of them appear to have reached near feature parity with relatively low spend.
storyTitle: Twilio S-1
outcome: IPO'd in 2016; $4.46B revenue and 325K customer accounts in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Twilio went public in June 2016 and grew into a communications platform with $4.46 billion in 2024 revenue and more than 325,000 active customer accounts. Pricing pressure was real, but Twilio's developer ecosystem and product breadth kept it at the center of the market.
note: The commodity risk was real—Twilio's gross margins and stock have been punished. It still built a much larger business than the 'low barrier' framing suggested.

author: tlianza
cardQuote: I don't think the people who jump ship are necessarily hyper-price-sensitive customers. Amazon is just turning this service into a commodity.
quote: To be fair, the price isn't just slightly lower - it is nearly an order of magnitude lower. Sending 500k messages a month with Amazon is $50, and with SendGrid it's $400. If you send that level of email a month (which is easy to do if you send a weekly newsletter to a few hundred thousand users) you're now talking about saving yourself a few grand a year with Amazon. Given the "switch" can be as simple as changing some SMTP settings, this is a big deal. I don't think the people who jump ship are necessarily hyper-price-sensitive customers. Amazon is just turning this service into a commodity.
storyTitle: SendGrid Responds to Amazon's Simple Email Service
outcome: IPO'd in 2017; acquired by Twilio for $3B in 2019.
outcomeDetail: SendGrid went public in 2017 and was acquired by Twilio in a deal valued at about $3 billion in 2019. It kept growing by selling deliverability, analytics, and developer tooling on top of commodity email.
note: The commoditization call was correct. SendGrid's answer was to move up the stack, not to win on raw SMTP pricing.

author: teyc
cardQuote: Parse is a distraction for FB. You are not even in the same business. Regardless of what you say, you are unable to override the CEO if or when he decides that Parse is to be shut down.
quote: Parse is a distraction for FB. You are not even in the same business. Regardless of what you say, you are unable to override the CEO if or when he decides that Parse is to be shut down. The alternatives are more appealing because their business model solely depends on customers paying for the back end service. The best thing FB can do is to bind itself legally to continue to run Parse for the next x number of years. If FB wants to dabble with PaaS, businesses are going to assess Parse on the basis that it is only an experiment. Tying oneself to a back end is like marriage. No one will invest in a relationship if the other side is only half serious.
storyTitle: Facebook buys Parse
outcome: Shut down by Facebook in January 2017.
outcomeDetail: Facebook bought Parse in 2013 and announced in 2016 that it would retire the service. Parse shut down in January 2017, though its platform was open-sourced for self-hosting.
note: The lock-in warning was exactly right. Parse's developers had to migrate or run the open-source fork.

author: aalpbalkan

quote: Classic TC title "to Take on AWS"... Don't make me laugh buddy. AWS is probably more than 1,000+ people operation with 30 different products and a marketplace, support and ops teams. DigitalOcean is purely a VM seller with no cloud or storage features.
storyTitle: DigitalOcean Raises $37.2M From Andreessen Horowitz to Take on AWS
outcome: IPO'd on the NYSE in 2021 at a ~$5B valuation.
outcomeDetail: DigitalOcean went public in March 2021 and raised $775 million. It carved out a durable business serving developers and small businesses that wanted simple, cheap cloud infrastructure.
note: The feature gap was real. DigitalOcean's bet was that a large segment of the market wanted fewer knobs, not more.

author: WorldWideWayne

The reason it uses more memory is because it has to do more. Because it has to do more, it's always going to be slower. So far on Fedora 21, VSCode is a slow and buggy experience. As a matter of fact, I can't think of one application developed with web tech that performs as well as it's native counterpart.
storyTitle: Microsoft Launches Visual Studio Code, a Free Cross-Platform Code Editor
outcome: Most-used IDE: 74% of developers in Stack Overflow's 2024 survey.
outcomeDetail: VS Code became the default editor for a generation of developers, with 74% usage in Stack Overflow's 2024 survey—more than twice its nearest competitor. Microsoft open-sourced it in 2015.
note: The beta was slow. Electron's performance improved, and the extension ecosystem turned the weakness into a platform.

storyTitle: GraphQL Working Draft
outcome: Adopted by GitHub, Shopify, Netflix; GraphQL Foundation formed in 2018.
outcomeDetail: GraphQL became a standard API layer, with production users including GitHub, Shopify, Netflix, Twitter, and The New York Times. The Linux Foundation formed the GraphQL Foundation in 2018.
note: The complexity warning was fair; GraphQL does add layers. The ecosystem built those layers quickly and standardized them.

storyTitle: PagerDuty (YC S10) Raises $10.7M From Andreessen Horowitz For IT Alert Service
outcome: IPO'd on the NYSE in 2019; ~$3B valuation on debut.
outcomeDetail: PagerDuty went public in April 2019 and popped nearly 60% on its first day, giving it a valuation close to $3 billion. It turned alert routing into a category and reached more than 11,000 customers by IPO.
note: The 'just alert coalescing' read missed the on-call scheduling, escalation, and integrations that make incident response a product.

author: mdeeks

storyTitle: Prometheus: An open-source service monitoring system and time series database
outcome: Graduated from CNCF in 2018; the standard for cloud-native monitoring.
outcomeDetail: Prometheus became the second CNCF project to graduate, after Kubernetes, in August 2018. Its pull model and PromQL became the default way to monitor containerized infrastructure.
note: Horizontal scaling was genuinely painful in early Prometheus. Federation and remote storage addressed it, and the Kubernetes ecosystem standardized on the rest.

storyTitle: Show HN: Netlify – Builds, Deploys and Hosts Your Static Site or App
outcome: Valued at $2B in 2021; 2M+ developers.
outcomeDetail: Netlify turned the static-site workflow into a product, with continuous deployment, previews, and edge hosting. It was valued at $2 billion in 2021 and reported more than two million developers using the platform.
note: The DIY stack worked for developers who enjoyed assembling it. Netlify sold the assembly, plus the workflow, to everyone else.

storyTitle: Algolia (YC W14) raises a $18.3M Series A
outcome: Valued at $2.25B in 2021; 10,000+ customers.
outcomeDetail: Algolia kept its usage-based pricing and grew into a search-as-a-service platform used by more than 10,000 companies. It raised $150 million at a $2.25 billion valuation in 2021.
note: The free tier really was small. Algolia's bet was that developers who outgrew it would rather pay than run Elasticsearch themselves.

author: rajatchopra
cardQuote: The one thing that will surely happen with this is that the code written will be 'locked in' to run only on aws territory.
quote: Good stuff. Basically it seems to do the bind+listen for you if you are the trigger subscriber. If you are the trigger generator, then it does socket.write for you. But the big deal is that you dont pay for 'listen', just pay for the function execution. The one thing that will surely happen with this is that the code written will be 'locked in' to run only on aws territory.
storyTitle: AWS Lambda
outcome: Became the standard serverless platform; every major cloud launched a Lambda-style service.
outcomeDetail: Lambda launched in 2014 and made event-driven, pay-per-execution computing mainstream. Serverless became a default architecture on AWS and spawned imitators across every cloud.
note: Vendor lock-in was a fair warning. It did not stop Lambda from becoming the reference implementation of serverless.

author: staunch
cardQuote: Still, it doesn't seem like it would save me enough time to warrant implementing your API, dealing with yet-another-service, and paying.
quote: I don't like to do everything myself. I'm actually very inclined to outsource stuff like this. It doesn't sound very interesting for sending email. The receiving part is more interesting. Still, it doesn't seem like it would save me enough time to warrant implementing your API, dealing with yet-another-service, and paying. I don't mean to be too negative. storyTitle: Mailgun (YC W11) Raises $1.1 Million For Its "Twilio For Email"
outcome: Acquired by Rackspace, then part of Sinch's $1.9B Pathwire deal.
outcomeDetail: Mailgun was acquired by Rackspace in 2012 and later became part of Pathwire, which Sinch bought for about $1.9 billion in 2021. It remained a major transactional email API, delivering hundreds of billions of emails a year.
note: The 'yet-another-service' objection underestimated how much developers would pay to avoid running mail servers.
